query: Consider the following context: The combination of elevated temperature and tribo-corrosion leads to the accelerated degradation of structural components used in many extreme environments. Recently developed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple principal elements have the potential for superior degradation resistance compared with presently used structural alloys. In that context, which material can be used for superior tribo-corrosion degradation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A high-entropy alloy that is pre-engineered by a controlled surface treatment (via thermal oxidation or laser surface processing) will form and stabilize a continuous, self‐healing spinel/oxide surface layer that significantly improves its resistance to degradation under combined high-temperature and tribological (wear-corrosion) conditions compared to untreated HEAs and conventional structural alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast or conventionally processed HEA (e.g., one based on Al, Co, Cr, Fe, Ni with Ti additions) with native surface oxidation but without deliberate surface engineering.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal oxidation or laser surface treatment to deliberately induce and stabilize the formation of a protective, self-healing spinel/oxide layer on the HEA surface.
generation.conditions: High-temperature environments (in the range where stable spinel phases form, e.g., ~600–1000 °C) combined with tribological stress that induces wear and mechanical damage.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, adherent spinel/oxide layer that forms in situ and can self-repair micro-damage, thereby acting as an effective diffusion barrier at the surface.
generation.mechanism: The pre-engineered protective oxide layer reduces the exposure of the underlying alloy to corrosive species and minimizes wear by providing a robust diffusion barrier. Its self-healing ability helps to continuously restore the barrier function after localized damage during sliding or impact.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in tribo-corrosion degradation rates (i.e., lower wear and corrosion loss over time) relative to untreated HEAs and conventional structural alloys under identical high-temperature and tribological conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated HEAs or traditional structural alloys exposed to similar elevated-temperature and wear-corrosion environments.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected within temperatures and mechanical stress conditions that permit stable spinel formation; extreme deviations in temperature, chemical environment, or mechanical load may exceed the self-healing capability of the oxide layer.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of improvement and the long-term durability of the engineered oxide layer under cyclic loading and varied environmental conditions remain uncertain and require systematic evaluation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the candidate HEA with the engineered surface treatment (controlled thermal oxidation or laser processing) and one set of untreated HEA. Subject both sets to identical cyclic high-temperature tribo-corrosion testing using a sliding wear apparatus combined with a corrosive medium. Monitor the degradation by periodic weight loss measurements, microscopic surface analysis, and phase identification via XRD or Raman spectroscopy to evaluate the integrity of the oxide layer.
measurements: Corrosion depth and pit formation (via surface profilometry)
Structural and phase composition of the surface layer (using XRD, Raman spectroscopy, or SEM-EDS)
Adhesion and self-healing capability of the oxide layer (using in situ or ex situ microscopic observation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the engineered HEA does not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in wear and corrosion rates relative to untreated samples under the test conditions, or if the pre-formed oxide layer fails to remain continuous or self-heal after damage, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

decision.trend: Early studies on HEAs primarily focused on controlling bulk microstructure and phase stability through compositional tuning and processing methods, which improved oxidation and general corrosion resistance. Over time, research such as the work on AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 showed that under elevated temperatures and tribological conditions, beneficial surface transformations—like the in situ formation of protective spinel phases—emerged and led to decreased wear. This progression indicates researchers moved from optimizing overall alloy composition and bulk processing to noting that surface phenomena under extreme environments can play a key role in mitigating tribo-corrosion degradation.
decision.unsolved: Despite improvements in bulk properties and the incidental formation of protective oxides at high temperatures, there remains a gap in deliberately designing and stabilizing a robust, self-healing surface layer that can concurrently combat both wear and corrosion under coupled high-temperature tribological stress.
decision.lever: Employ controlled thermal oxidation or laser surface treatment to induce and stabilize a continuous, self-healing spinel/oxide layer on the HEA surface
decision.why: This approach builds on the observed trend that beneficial oxide phases (such as spinels) form under high-temperature tribo-wear conditions. By deliberately engineering the surface to optimize this protective film, the material can better resist the synergistic effects of wear and corrosion, directly addressing the unsolved challenge identified in the current state of research.
